name: Pulsed dye laser for stretch marks

lead: Pulsed dye laser is an in-office treatment used on new red or purple stretch marks to reduce redness before they fade to white. Skin-focused communities use it to make marks from growth, pregnancy, weight or muscle gain less visible.

The laser light is absorbed by hemoglobin in the small vessels of early marks, which proponents say reduces the redness. Published research is small: one registered 2024 trial of 20 people compares it with carboxytherapy, with no results listed. Broader reviews cited by Wikipedia report that no stretch-mark treatment has been clearly shown effective once marks have formed.

paras: Treatment is done by clinicians in a series of sessions spaced weeks apart. It is aimed at early red marks, and results for older white marks are described as more limited.
The sources reviewed give no safety data for this use. Laser procedures are performed by clinicians, and they can cause redness, swelling and pigment changes on the treated skin.

angle.text: The laser targets blood vessels in fresh red or purple stretch marks, so their redness fades and they stand out less. Trials are small, and it is used on early marks rather than older white ones.

lead: Pulsed dye laser (PDL) treatment for stretch marks (striae distensae) is an in-office procedure in which a laser emitting light absorbed by blood vessels is applied to early, red or purple stretch marks (striae rubra). It is discussed in looksmaxxing and skin-focused communities as a way to reduce the redness of newly formed marks before they fade to white.

Stretch marks form when the dermis is torn or stretched during pregnancy, growth spurts, or weight and muscle gain, and begin as reddish or purple lesions that later become pale and atrophic [1]. Wikipedia's article on stretch marks, citing a 2014 systematic review, states that no treatment has been clearly shown to be useful once marks have formed, and it does not specifically discuss pulsed dye laser [1].

Published trial registrations show that PDL continues to be studied, for example against carboxytherapy in red stretch marks in a small 20-person study registered in 2024, with no results listed in the registry entry [2].
infobox: Early red or purple stretch marks (striae rubra)

paras: Pulsed dye lasers emit short pulses of light that are preferentially absorbed by hemoglobin. Proponents therefore apply them to striae rubra, in which dilated blood vessels contribute to the red or purple colour, rather than to older white marks. The sources reviewed for this article do not describe device settings, and none are given here.

Stretch marks are commonly attributed to mechanical stretching of the skin, with elevated cortisol and corticosteroid exposure proposed as contributing factors [1]. Marks begin reddish or purple and later lose pigment [1]. Treatments that have been tried include tretinoin and hyaluronic acid (reported effective on early marks in some studies), various lasers, carboxytherapy and micrografting, but Wikipedia summarises the overall evidence as lacking a clearly useful treatment [1].

A registered trial, NCT06591208, started in September 2024 and enrolling 20 participants, compares pulsed dye laser with carboxytherapy in striae rubra; its status was listed as unknown and no results were available in the registry record [2]. No other trials or published outcomes for PDL in stretch marks were examined for this article, so the effect size is not characterised here.

The procedure appears in skin and body-improvement discussions as an option for fresh stretch marks, usually alongside other treatments. No forum material was available for this entry, so community claims are not documented in detail.

timeline.event: A trial comparing pulsed dye laser with carboxytherapy for striae rubra is registered (NCT06591208). [2]
